questions.q: What is the key functional difference between a Profile Login IP Range and an org-wide Trusted IP Range?
options: They are the same setting under two different names
A Login IP Range actually blocks logins from outside the range; a Trusted IP Range only skips the extra identity-verification challenge and doesn't block anything by itself
Trusted IP Range blocks logins, while Login IP Range only skips a challenge
Login IP Range only applies to API calls, never to UI logins
questions.explain: Profile Login IP Range is an access-blocking control. Trusted IP Range is different -- it lets a login from a listed address skip the extra verification challenge, but a login from outside it isn't blocked by this setting alone, just challenged further.

questions.q: What does the org-wide session setting 'Enforce login IP ranges on every request' change about Profile Login IP Range behavior?
options: It extends the check beyond login to every subsequent request, cutting off a session mid-stream if the client's IP falls outside the range
It applies Login IP Range restrictions only to Trusted IP Ranges
It only affects connected apps, never direct UI logins
It disables Login IP Range checking entirely
questions.explain: By default the Login IP Range check happens at login only. Enabling this org-wide setting extends enforcement to every request, so a session started from an allowed IP gets cut off the moment the client's IP falls outside the range, even mid-session.

questions.q: Which OAuth flows does this lesson identify as always enforcing IP restrictions, regardless of the connected app's IP relaxation setting?
options: Authorization Code and Client Credentials
Only the Username-Password flow
None -- all OAuth flows respect the connected app's relaxation setting equally
JWT Bearer and SAML Bearer
questions.explain: JWT Bearer and SAML Bearer flows are a specific exception: they always enforce IP restrictions no matter what relaxation policy is set on the connected app, so the integration's source IP must actually fall within the applicable Login IP Range or Trusted IP Range.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend scoping an integration's Login IP Range to its known, stable source IPs rather than leaving it unrestricted?
options: It has no real security benefit, it's only a performance optimization
Unrestricted IP ranges are not technically possible to configure in Salesforce

It shrinks the integration's attack surface by blocking or challenging login attempts with that credential from anywhere else, which matters because an unattended integration won't notice an unfamiliar login prompt the way a human would
It is required before API Enabled can be granted
questions.explain: Because an integration credential is unattended (Lesson 1), scoping its allowed source IPs closes off one more avenue of misuse if the credential is ever exposed -- a stolen credential used from an unexpected location gets blocked or challenged rather than silently working.

questions.q: What operational risk does this lesson flag when an integration's Login IP Range is scoped tightly to known vendor IPs?
options: Tight IP scoping disables the integration's ability to use OAuth entirely

If the vendor's infrastructure changes (e.g. migrates to new egress IPs), the integration will break the moment its source IP falls outside the configured range, so the range needs periodic review tied to infrastructure changes
There is no risk; once configured correctly it never needs revisiting
Tightly scoped IP ranges automatically expire after 90 days
questions.explain: A tightly scoped IP range is a trade-off: it shrinks attack surface but also means the integration breaks if its actual source IPs change, so the range needs to be reviewed whenever the integration's own infrastructure changes, not set once and forgotten.
